items.title: RAG vs. retriever-free RAG, clearly explained!
items.summary:
RAG vs. retriever-free RAG, clearly explained!

(powered by decision models like Jev)

In a standard RAG setup, documents are split into chunks, converted into embeddings, and stored in a vector index.

When a query arrives, the system embeds it and pulls the top-k chunks with the closest vectors.

A reranker then reorders those candidates against the query, and the best few go to the LLM as context.

The problem is that the similarity search decides what the LLM can ever see.

If the right passage never made the top-k, nothing later in the pipeline can bring it back, not even a strong reranker.

Retriever-free RAG, from a new Cornell and ASAPP paper, keeps the documents and the LLM but replaces similarity search with navigation.

The documents are organized as a document tree, like a table of contents, and a decision model (Jev 1.13) walks down it.

A decision model doesn't generate text. It reads one shared context and returns a probability for every yes/no question about it, in one forward pass per stage.

Here's how a query moves through the tree:

↳ Top documents: the model reads the query beside every candidate document, asks "Is this relevant?" for each, and keeps the best few.
↳ Top passages: it opens only those documents and asks the same question for every passage inside them.
↳ Most relevant? (optional): a single multiple-choice question reorders the top 20 passages (top 5 on Natural Questions).

Dropped documents are never opened, so their passages are never scored.

On Natural Questions (2.68M Wikipedia paragraphs), its top pick contained the answer 65.4% of the time. Embedding search plus an 8B reranker got 48.0%, and GPT-5 reranking got 60.8%.

The gain comes from ranking, not coverage. Embedding search's top 100 holds the answer more often than the navigated shortlist (98.4% vs 94.0%), but navigation is better at putting it first.

Median retrieval takes under 2 seconds per query, but each method was timed in a different setup, so it isn't a controlled speed comparison.

The main limit is that it needs a sensible hierarchy, and a document pruned early is gone for good. It also skips embedding search only at query time, since the Wikipedia tree was built offline using embeddings.

The diagram below depicts the complete flow.

- RAG retrieves by similarity, then reranks.
- Retriever-free RAG navigates a document tree with a decision model.
- The LLM answers from the top passages.

If you're building a RAG system, this is worth benchmarking against your current setup.

Here's the paper: https://t.co/U7cCcIfZV1

If you're new to decision models, I've quoted my full breakdown of how Jev works below.

items.title: New model helps robots learn tasks faster with less human programming
items.summary:
Called agentic robotics, the approach allows teams of AI agents to generate robot-control programs, test them in simulated environments, identify failures, and revise their code before deploying it on physical machines.

The technology could address two longstanding challenges in robotics: the extensive engineering required to program robot behaviors and the large volumes of real-world data needed to train robots through imitation learning. [...] Agentic robotics seeks to combine the advantages of these methods while reducing their limitations. The approach uses a framework called Graph-as-Policy, which divides complex robotic tasks into smaller, reusable skills. These include identifying objects, planning grasps, and moving robotic grippers without colliding with surrounding objects. [...] UC Berkeley researchers have developed an AI-driven approach that could significantly accelerate how robots are programmed and trained for real-world tasks. Called agentic robotics, the approach uses teams of AI agents to generate robot-control programs, test them in simulated environments, and refine their performance.

The method could reduce the need for extensive training data and manual engineering, two major challenges that have slowed the development of capable robots.

items.title: Robots could transform breast surgery forever | Vox
items.summary:
In a traditional mastectomy, the surgical cut is held physically open with instruments called retractors, which can cause considerable physical trauma and pressure in the area around it. By contrast, in robotic surgery, carbon dioxide gas is used to open up the space in a much gentler manner. Farr believes that reduced trauma to the skin and better visualization of structures (and hence increased ability to avoid critical nerves) in robot-assisted surgery could be the reason that some patients [...] In a robotic mastectomy, the surgeon sits at a console a few feet away from the patient and controls every movement of the machine’s instruments with their hands. The da Vinci single-port robot, the version cleared for nipple-sparing mastectomies, has one arm that enters the body through a single small incision usually along the side of the chest or, in some cases, in the fold beneath the breast. The arm has three multi-jointed instruments at one end, which the surgeon can use to bend, grasp, [...] Some surgeons are embracing this new technology because it offers a smaller, hidden scar and a clearer view inside the breast. Some patients also report better sensation in the chest area afterward.
 But critics say that there isn’t conclusive long-term evidence yet that robotic nipple-sparing mastectomies are as good as open mastectomies at making sure the cancer doesn’t come back, even if they are technically safe to perform.

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.
